quizzes.stem: An assistant is asked to tally the letter r in a long part number and gives a wrong, confident figure. The team wants a fix that holds for every part number. Which approach is best?

options.a: Ask it to spell the part number out letter by letter before answering
options.b: Hand the counting to a small script and use its output
options.c: Move to a model with a larger context window available
options.d: Run the same question five times and take the most common figure

explanation.b: The model works on pieces, not letters, so a character-level tally is an approximation and a small program answers it exactly (the tokenizer section and the first trap).
explanation.a: Ruled out because "The model never sees the letters of lowest as six separate things", so a spelled-out version is itself produced from pieces.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "The window is how much text fits per request", a capacity that does not change how a part number is cut into pieces.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "a model answers it by approximation", so repeating the question repeats the approximation.

quizzes.stem: A team corrects the assistant by hand after it repeats a mistake across many chats, and expects it to do better next week. They call the API directly and store no history. Which expectation is accurate?

options.a: The weights absorb the fix and apply it to every later session by default
options.b: The API stores the fix under the account's key for reuse
options.c: Only a request that carries the amended guidance in its own input can benefit
options.d: Memory features retrain the weights whenever a user saves a note

explanation.c: Weights are fixed at inference and what looks like learning is the context window (the weights section), so only a call that carries the fix in its input can use it.
explanation.a: Ruled out because "A conversation with Claude does not teach it anything that carries to the next conversation".
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Changing the weights is a separate act from calling the model", so an API call stores nothing for later.
explanation.d: Ruled out because memory features work by putting notes back: "saved notes are put back into the context", and the weights stay as they were.

quizzes.stem: A stakeholder asks why a deployed assistant answers a question with an answer, when the raw model it started from tends to continue the question with more questions. Which part of how models are made does most to explain the gap?

options.a: Pretraining on a far larger corpus than the raw model saw
options.b: A larger attention mechanism that lets the model reread the question
options.c: A separate look-up store of answers that the assistant consults
options.d: A later round of tuning on curated examples and replies ranked by people

explanation.d: Fine-tuning and feedback training are the stages that turn a text continuer into an assistant (the stages section).
explanation.a: Ruled out because the stage list says of pretraining that "The result is capable and unruly", and a bigger corpus does not change that.
explanation.b: Ruled out because in attention "every position in the context can look at every earlier position", in the raw model as much as in the assistant.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "There is no third place such as a notebook it consults": everything the model uses is in the window or in the weights.

quizzes.stem: A company wants Claude to answer from its product manual, which is revised every month, through the Claude API. An engineer proposes fine-tuning on each new version. What is the best response?

options.a: Include the current edition in every call, since the context is the standard route
options.b: Go ahead with monthly tuning, then patch the gaps through corrections made in chat
options.c: Tune the model once on the manual so its weights keep the facts for good
options.d: Place the edition in the prompt and also tune the model, to be safe

explanation.a: Knowledge that changes monthly belongs in the context, and the glossary says the Claude API does not currently offer fine-tuning (the second trap and the table).
explanation.b: Ruled out because the table lists "Memory of your previous conversations" among the things training does not give, so chat corrections patch nothing.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the table credits training with "Broad general knowledge to a cut-off date" and nothing newer, so weights cannot track a monthly revision.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "the Claude API does not currently offer fine-tuning", so the added step is not available through this route.

quizzes.stem: An analyst taught Claude a set of internal abbreviations in a chat last week. In a new chat today it ignores them, and the analyst concludes something broke. Which explanation fits?

options.a: Unfamiliar abbreviations were split into odd pieces, so the model could not match them again
options.b: Weights stay fixed in use, so the earlier session left nothing behind to reuse
options.c: The context window filled up last week, so the oldest abbreviations were pushed out
options.d: Chats feed a nightly fine-tuning round, and this week's round skipped the abbreviations

explanation.b: Weights do not change while you chat, so a new conversation has no trace of the old one (page 1, weights section).
explanation.a: Ruled out because the tokenizer copes with unseen text, since "a word the corpus never contained, still encodes, from smaller pieces", and the model only needs the abbreviations in its input (page 1).
explanation.c: Ruled out because "what looks like learning inside one conversation is the context window doing its job", and a new chat starts with an empty window (page 1).
explanation.d: Ruled out because "A conversation with Claude does not teach it anything that carries to the next conversation", so no nightly round learns from chats (page 1).

quizzes.stem: A localisation lead notices that one paragraph needs noticeably more tokens in one language than in another. Which explanation fits best?

options.a: The model silently translates the harder language before reading it, which adds pieces
options.b: Preference training from human rankings sets how many pieces each language costs
options.c: Its learned vocabulary stores longer chunks for the script that dominated the corpus
options.d: The translated text simply contains more words, and tokens track words one to one

explanation.c: The vocabulary was learned from a corpus, so a script that was common gets longer pieces and a rarer one splits into more (page 1, what the tokenizer does to your work).
explanation.a: Ruled out because "text must be cut into pieces and each piece mapped to an integer" before the model reads anything, so the count is set by the cutting and not by a hidden translation step (page 1).
explanation.b: Ruled out because the tokenizer is "built before pretraining and fixed afterwards", so later feedback training cannot change what a language costs (page 1).
explanation.d: Ruled out because a token is not a word: "a Claude token is about 3.5 English characters", and "the exact number can vary depending on the language used" (page 1).

quizzes.stem: A reviewer waves through a number in a report because the assistant is built to be honest. Which reply is the soundest?

options.a: Honesty goals cover harmful topics only, so numbers are exempt
options.b: A system prompt can switch the honesty framework on for a task
options.c: Honesty work verifies each figure against its sources before release
options.d: That describes a goal, not a guarantee, so key claims still need checking

explanation.d: The glossary frames HHH as how Claude is trained, and the first trap says verification is still the user's job.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the honest part of HHH means "an honest one gives accurate information and acknowledges" its limits, so it reaches beyond harmful topics.
explanation.b: Ruled out because "an instruction that fights the training may not win", so a system prompt cannot switch a training framework on.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the table lists "A guarantee that any statement is true" among the things training does not give.

quizzes.stem: A team is automating four chores. Which one should be done by a deterministic program instead of the model alone?

options.a: Verifying every product code is exactly eight characters long
options.b: Rewriting release notes for a non-technical audience of customers
options.c: Proposing likely causes for an intermittent failing test
options.d: Sorting incoming emails by urgency from the message text

explanation.a: Exact character work is a tokenizer-level weakness, so code should do it (page 1, first trap).
explanation.b: Ruled out because the table credits training with "Fluent language, many languages, code", which covers rewording for customers.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the table credits training with "Reasoning patterns it can apply to new problems", which covers proposing causes.
explanation.d: Ruled out because the table lists "Following instructions and a helpful manner", and a model reads message text well.
